platforms.title: It's Not the Heat — It's How You Cool Down Before Bed
platforms.meta_description: Struggling to sleep through a tropical night? The real problem may not be the heat itself but three habits that stop your core body temperature from dropping.
platforms.body_html:
Lying awake through a tropical night with the air conditioner already running is a familiar kind of frustration. What actually decides whether you fall asleep, though, isn't just the room temperature — it's how well your core body temperature manages to drop. Three ordinary evening habits quietly block that drop and make sweltering nights feel even harder to sleep through.

Why a Dropping Core Temperature Matters So Much

Just before sleep onset, blood vessels in your hands and feet widen so your body can release heat from its core outward, and that release needs to lower your core temperature by roughly one degree Celsius before your brain properly registers the signal to fall asleep. On a tropical night when the temperature never drops below 25°C, that heat release is already sluggish — and three habits can stall it almost completely.

First is a cold shower right before bed. Cold water feels like instant relief, but it actually triggers your sympathetic nervous system, narrowing blood vessels and raising your heart rate — which keeps blood away from your hands and feet instead of letting heat escape through them. A 2019 meta-analysis by researchers at the University of Texas at Austin, published in the journal Sleep Medicine Reviews, found that a warm bath or shower at around 40 to 42.5°C taken one to two hours before bedtime helped people fall asleep roughly ten minutes faster on average, because the warm water widens blood vessels in the extremities and helps core heat escape more efficiently.

Second is scrolling on a phone before bed. Blue-wavelength light from screens suppresses melatonin, and according to Harvard Medical School research, blue light suppresses melatonin roughly twice as long as green light and shifts your circadian rhythm about twice as much. Third is afternoon caffeine. Caffeine's half-life is roughly five to six hours, so a cup of coffee at 2 or 3 p.m. can still leave nearly half its dose active in your system by 9 or 10 p.m., keeping you more alert than you realize, even when you feel exhausted enough to fall asleep instantly.

Cool Down the Right Way Before You Try to Sleep

Take your shower one to two hours before bed, using warm water around 40°C for five to ten minutes instead of cold water. Put your phone out of reach starting thirty minutes before bedtime, and switch to dim, warm lighting instead of bright white lights. Cut off coffee by 2 p.m., and swap anything caffeinated in the evening for plain water or a caffeine-free herbal tea instead.

If sweltering nights keep leaving you exhausted for weeks even after adjusting these habits, or your lack of sleep starts interfering with work or daily functioning, it's worth talking to a doctor rather than continuing to push through it — persistent insomnia can have underlying causes that these habit changes alone won't fix. It's also worth mentioning a bedroom fan or a cooling mat to a doctor if the room itself simply can't be brought down to a comfortable temperature overnight, since airflow across the skin speeds up that same heat-releasing process described above.
